title: Low-rank misalignment subspace in CLIP patch tokens
one_line_idea: Test whether the patch-level text misalignment of contrastively trained VLMs is concentrated in a low-rank subspace induced by global pooling, removable by a closed-form projection without any training.
problem: CLIP-style models align global image embeddings with text but their patch tokens are poorly aligned, and every fix so far retrains or fine-tunes the encoder.
core_hypothesis: The pooling objective pushes a small number of directions in patch space toward image-global content; projecting those directions out restores most of the latent patch-text alignment at zero training cost.
falsifiable_prediction: A rank-k projection (k small, e.g. under 16) estimated from unlabeled images closes a large fraction of the dense zero-shot mIoU gap between raw patch readout and trained dense-alignment methods; if the gap barely moves for any small k, the hypothesis is dead.
why_important: A closed-form fix would make every existing CLIP checkpoint usable for dense tasks and would explain mechanistically why dense alignment methods work.
why_possibly_novel: Training-free dense readouts exist, but a causal low-rank account tied to the pooling objective, with a closed-form removal recipe, is not something I can point to as established; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate top principal directions separating patch tokens from text-aligned space on unlabeled data; project them out; evaluate zero-shot segmentation on two datasets against raw readout and a trained baseline.
main_risk: Misalignment may be high-rank and token-dependent, in which case no small projection helps.
community_default_belief: Dense alignment requires additional training (fine-tuning, self-distillation, or auxiliary dense losses) because contrastive pretraining fundamentally discards spatial alignment.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The contrastive loss only constrains the pooled vector, so patch tokens may retain aligned structure that is merely masked by a few pooling-oriented directions rather than destroyed.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One afternoon test: PCA on patch-minus-text residuals for one CLIP model, project out top-8 directions, measure zero-shot mIoU delta on one segmentation set; near-zero delta kills it.
core_claim: The pooling objective pushes a small number of directions in patch space toward image-global content; projecting those directions out restores most of the latent patch-text alignment at zero training cost.
method_sketch: Estimate top principal directions separating patch tokens from text-aligned space on unlabeled data; project them out; evaluate zero-shot segmentation on two datasets against raw readout and a trained baseline.
novelty_hook: Training-free dense readouts exist, but a causal low-rank account tied to the pooling objective, with a closed-form removal recipe, is not something I can point to as established; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Misalignment may be high-rank and token-dependent, in which case no small projection helps.

title: Patch-level modality gap grows with depth
one_line_idea: Measure how the image-text modality gap behaves at patch granularity across encoder depth and test whether the best dense readout layer is predictable from the gap curve alone.
problem: Dense VLM methods pick which layer to read features from by trial and error, with no principled selection rule.
core_hypothesis: The patch-to-text modality gap has a characteristic depth profile whose minimum coincides with the empirically best dense readout layer, making layer choice predictable without labels.
falsifiable_prediction: Across at least three VLM families, the layer minimizing a label-free patch-text gap statistic matches the layer maximizing dense zero-shot mIoU within one layer; frequent mismatches falsify the rule.
why_important: A label-free layer-selection rule removes a hidden hyperparameter from every dense VLM pipeline and yields a diagnostic of where alignment lives.
why_possibly_novel: The modality gap is studied at the global embedding level; a per-layer patch-granularity treatment used as a practical layer selector appears unexplored to my knowledge; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute per-layer patch-text gap statistics on unlabeled images for three model families; separately sweep dense zero-shot performance per layer; report rank correlation between the two orderings.
main_risk: The gap statistic may be dominated by norm artifacts rather than alignment, breaking the correlation.
community_default_belief: Final or penultimate layer features are the right dense readout, and layer choice is a minor detail.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Depth-wise specialization in ViTs means alignment-relevant structure can peak mid-network, and the final layers may be specialized for pooling rather than spatial fidelity.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Single model, one dataset: plot gap-vs-depth and mIoU-vs-depth; if the curves visibly disagree on the optimum, the rule fails its first test.
core_claim: The patch-to-text modality gap has a characteristic depth profile whose minimum coincides with the empirically best dense readout layer, making layer choice predictable without labels.
method_sketch: Compute per-layer patch-text gap statistics on unlabeled images for three model families; separately sweep dense zero-shot performance per layer; report rank correlation between the two orderings.
novelty_hook: The modality gap is studied at the global embedding level; a per-layer patch-granularity treatment used as a practical layer selector appears unexplored to my knowledge; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: The gap statistic may be dominated by norm artifacts rather than alignment, breaking the correlation.

title: Artifact tokens as the main corruptor of dense text alignment
one_line_idea: Quantify how much of the dense zero-shot gap in VLMs is attributable to high-norm artifact tokens rather than to genuinely unaligned patch content.
problem: ViT encoders develop high-norm outlier tokens that carry global information, and their effect on pixel-text alignment is not isolated from other causes of dense failure.
core_hypothesis: A disproportionate share of dense zero-shot errors is caused by artifact tokens contaminating local similarity maps, so detecting and masking them recovers most of the gap to register-trained models.
falsifiable_prediction: Masking or inpainting detected outlier tokens at inference improves dense zero-shot mIoU by a margin comparable to retraining with register tokens; if masking yields only marginal gains, artifact tokens are not the bottleneck.
why_important: It would separate an architectural artifact from a representational deficiency, redirecting effort away from expensive retraining when a readout-level fix suffices.
why_possibly_novel: Registers and artifacts are documented; using artifact suppression as a controlled causal probe of pixel-text alignment specifically, with a quantified share of the gap, seems unreported; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Detect outlier tokens by norm on frozen CLIP-like models, replace them with neighborhood interpolation, and evaluate zero-shot segmentation before and after on two datasets, comparing against a register-pretrained control.
main_risk: Artifact tokens may be load-bearing for text alignment of neighboring tokens, so removal could hurt more than help.
community_default_belief: Dense zero-shot weakness of CLIP reflects missing spatial supervision, not fixable readout artifacts.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Documented high-norm token phenomena show global information intrudes into local tokens, which is exactly the failure mode that would corrupt local text similarity without any representational deficiency.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One model, one dataset, norm-threshold masking with bilinear infill; measure the mIoU delta in a day.
core_claim: A disproportionate share of dense zero-shot errors is caused by artifact tokens contaminating local similarity maps, so detecting and masking them recovers most of the gap to register-trained models.
method_sketch: Detect outlier tokens by norm on frozen CLIP-like models, replace them with neighborhood interpolation, and evaluate zero-shot segmentation before and after on two datasets, comparing against a register-pretrained control.
novelty_hook: Registers and artifacts are documented; using artifact suppression as a controlled causal probe of pixel-text alignment specifically, with a quantified share of the gap, seems unreported; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Artifact tokens may be load-bearing for text alignment of neighboring tokens, so removal could hurt more than help.

title: Saliency prior of contrastive pooling suppresses stuff classes
one_line_idea: Test whether CLIP attention pooling encodes an object-saliency prior that systematically under-aligns stuff regions (sky, road, grass) relative to things, explaining the stuff-things dense gap.
problem: Open-vocabulary segmentation consistently does worse on stuff categories, and the cause is usually attributed vaguely to data rather than to a measurable pooling mechanism.
core_hypothesis: Pooling attention weights concentrate on thing-like regions during pretraining, causing stuff patches to receive weaker alignment gradients, an effect measurable and partially reversible by reweighted readout.
falsifiable_prediction: Pooling attention mass over stuff regions is significantly lower than area-proportional, and a stuff-reweighted readout narrows the stuff-things mIoU gap; if attention mass is area-proportional, the mechanism is refuted.
why_important: It would identify a concrete training-signal asymmetry behind a well-known failure mode and suggest cheap correction levers at readout or pretraining time.
why_possibly_novel: The stuff-things gap is documented; attributing it causally to pooling attention statistics with an intervention seems unarticulated; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a dataset with stuff-things masks, compute pooling attention mass per region type for a frozen model, correlate with per-class dense zero-shot accuracy, then test a reweighted readout intervention.
main_risk: Stuff under-performance may be dominated by text-side issues (vague class names) rather than image-side pooling.
community_default_belief: Stuff classes lag because web captions rarely mention backgrounds, a data problem that only more data can fix.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Even in captioned data mentioning backgrounds, the pooled objective can ignore stuff regions; the bottleneck may be the pooling gradient path, not caption content.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Half-day: extract pooling attention maps for a few hundred images, compare stuff vs things attention mass against area; no asymmetry kills the mechanism.
core_claim: Pooling attention weights concentrate on thing-like regions during pretraining, causing stuff patches to receive weaker alignment gradients, an effect measurable and partially reversible by reweighted readout.
method_sketch: On a dataset with stuff-things masks, compute pooling attention mass per region type for a frozen model, correlate with per-class dense zero-shot accuracy, then test a reweighted readout intervention.
novelty_hook: The stuff-things gap is documented; attributing it causally to pooling attention statistics with an intervention seems unarticulated; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Stuff under-performance may be dominated by text-side issues (vague class names) rather than image-side pooling.

title: Text anisotropy predicts dense confusion structure
one_line_idea: Test whether pairwise text-embedding cosines among class names predict the pixel-level confusion matrix of open-vocabulary segmenters, making text-side whitening a cheaper fix than image fine-tuning.
problem: Dense open-vocab errors are treated as image-representation failures, but class-name text embeddings occupy a narrow anisotropic cone that may itself cause confusions.
core_hypothesis: A large fraction of inter-class pixel confusion variance is explained by text-embedding similarity alone, and decorrelating text embeddings reduces those confusions without touching the image encoder.
falsifiable_prediction: Regression from text cosine to confusion rate has strong explanatory power across datasets, and text whitening cuts the most text-confusable class pairs' errors measurably; weak correlation falsifies the premise.
why_important: If the text side is a first-order cause of dense errors, the community's focus on image-encoder fine-tuning is misallocated for a class of failures.
why_possibly_novel: Text-embedding anisotropy is known in NLP; using it to predict and repair pixel-level confusion matrices of segmenters seems unexplored; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For two open-vocab segmenters and two datasets, regress pixel confusion rates on text cosines, then apply whitening or contrastive text re-embedding and re-measure the confusion matrix.
main_risk: Confusions may be dominated by visual similarity that co-varies with text similarity, confounding the regression.
community_default_belief: Dense misclassification reflects insufficient visual grounding, so fixes belong on the image side.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Classification happens in the joint space, and an anisotropic text cone mathematically compresses decision margins regardless of visual feature quality.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One model, one dataset: scatter-plot class-pair text cosine vs confusion rate; absence of visible relationship ends the idea quickly.
core_claim: A large fraction of inter-class pixel confusion variance is explained by text-embedding similarity alone, and decorrelating text embeddings reduces those confusions without touching the image encoder.
method_sketch: For two open-vocab segmenters and two datasets, regress pixel confusion rates on text cosines, then apply whitening or contrastive text re-embedding and re-measure the confusion matrix.
novelty_hook: Text-embedding anisotropy is known in NLP; using it to predict and repair pixel-level confusion matrices of segmenters seems unexplored; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Confusions may be dominated by visual similarity that co-varies with text similarity, confounding the regression.

title: Dense alignment is a linear reparameterization, not new knowledge
one_line_idea: Test whether a single linear map per layer, fit on one dataset, transfers dense text alignment to unseen datasets as well as full dense fine-tuning does.
problem: Dense-alignment fine-tuning methods are assumed to teach VLMs new spatial knowledge, but they may only be re-basing existing features.
core_hypothesis: Frozen VLM patch features already linearly encode what dense fine-tuning surfaces, so a dataset-agnostic linear head captures most of the fine-tuning gain and transfers across domains.
falsifiable_prediction: A linear alignment head trained on dataset A retains most of its dense zero-shot gain on datasets B and C, within a small margin of full fine-tuning; large transfer loss falsifies the reparameterization view.
why_important: It would reframe a whole family of methods as readout calibration, drastically simplifying deployment and clarifying what pretraining already contains.
why_possibly_novel: Linear probing is standard, but a cross-dataset transfer test used specifically to adjudicate reparameterization-vs-new-knowledge for dense VLM alignment appears untested; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit linear patch-to-text maps on one dataset for two frozen VLMs; evaluate zero-shot on three unseen datasets against both raw readout and dense fine-tuned versions of the same models.
main_risk: Boundary-level improvements from fine-tuning may be inherently nonlinear and never captured by any linear head.
community_default_belief: Dense fine-tuning injects spatial grounding that contrastive pretraining lacks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Frozen-feature probes keep matching fine-tuned pipelines in adjacent tasks, suggesting information is present and methods differ mainly in readout.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Train the linear head on COCO-Stuff, test on ADE20K in one day; if the transferred head collapses toward raw-readout performance, reparameterization is wrong.
core_claim: Frozen VLM patch features already linearly encode what dense fine-tuning surfaces, so a dataset-agnostic linear head captures most of the fine-tuning gain and transfers across domains.
method_sketch: Fit linear patch-to-text maps on one dataset for two frozen VLMs; evaluate zero-shot on three unseen datasets against both raw readout and dense fine-tuned versions of the same models.
novelty_hook: Linear probing is standard, but a cross-dataset transfer test used specifically to adjudicate reparameterization-vs-new-knowledge for dense VLM alignment appears untested; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Boundary-level improvements from fine-tuning may be inherently nonlinear and never captured by any linear head.

title: Spatial smoothing confound in dense VLM method gains
one_line_idea: Quantify how much of reported training-free dense-VLM improvements is reproducible by a generic label-free spatial smoothing filter with no method-specific machinery.
problem: Many training-free dense readout methods change attention structure in ways that also smooth predictions spatially, and the two effects are never separated.
core_hypothesis: A generic smoothing operator (e.g. feature-space bilateral filtering of similarity maps) reproduces the majority of the gain of several published training-free dense readout tricks, implying their specific mechanisms matter less than claimed.
falsifiable_prediction: Generic smoothing recovers over half the mIoU improvement of representative attention-modification methods on standard benchmarks; if smoothing recovers little, mechanism-specific claims survive.
why_important: It would recalibrate how the community evaluates dense readout methods and force smoothing-controlled baselines.
why_possibly_novel: Smoothing-controlled ablations for this method family are not standard practice to my knowledge; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Reimplement two or three training-free dense readout methods, add a smoothing-only baseline tuned on a held-out split, and compare deltas over the raw readout on two benchmarks.
main_risk: Different methods may exceed smoothing by different amounts, giving a muddy answer rather than a clean confound story.
community_default_belief: Gains of attention-modification readouts come from correcting attention semantics, not from incidental spatial regularization.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense metrics reward spatial coherence heavily, so any operator increasing local label agreement gains mIoU regardless of semantic correction.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One benchmark, one method, one smoothing baseline: if smoothing alone matches the method, the confound is real; a day of compute.
core_claim: A generic smoothing operator (e.g. feature-space bilateral filtering of similarity maps) reproduces the majority of the gain of several published training-free dense readout tricks, implying their specific mechanisms matter less than claimed.
method_sketch: Reimplement two or three training-free dense readout methods, add a smoothing-only baseline tuned on a held-out split, and compare deltas over the raw readout on two benchmarks.
novelty_hook: Smoothing-controlled ablations for this method family are not standard practice to my knowledge; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Different methods may exceed smoothing by different amounts, giving a muddy answer rather than a clean confound story.

title: Negation collapse is measurable at the patch level
one_line_idea: Measure whether patch-text similarity maps for negated prompts (no person, without wheels) are near-identical to their positive counterparts, and locate where in the text encoder negation is lost.
problem: VLM text encoders are suspected to ignore negation, but the failure has mainly been shown at image level, not as a pixel-level alignment phenomenon with a localized cause.
core_hypothesis: Negated and positive prompts produce patch similarity maps with near-unity correlation because negation tokens are attenuated early in the text encoder, and a targeted text-side intervention can restore contrast.
falsifiable_prediction: Map correlation between negated and positive prompts exceeds a high threshold (predicting near 0.9) across models, and ablating identified negation-processing components changes it; low correlation falsifies negation collapse at pixel level.
why_important: Dense negation handling is a prerequisite for exclusion queries in interactive segmentation and safety-critical filtering, and locating the failure enables targeted fixes.
why_possibly_novel: Negation failure is documented for retrieval; a patch-level characterization with a text-encoder localization study appears missing; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build positive-negated prompt pairs over common categories, compute patch similarity map correlations for three VLMs, then run layer-wise text-encoder interventions to find where negation signal dies.
main_risk: Negation may be represented but overridden at the joint-similarity stage, making text-encoder localization misleading.
community_default_belief: Negation failure is a text-encoder capacity issue that only scale or better language pretraining fixes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The contrastive objective never rewards negation contrast, so the failure may be an objective-level artifact fixable with a small amount of targeted contrastive data rather than scale.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Fifty prompt pairs, one model, one afternoon: histogram of map correlations decides whether pixel-level negation collapse exists.
core_claim: Negated and positive prompts produce patch similarity maps with near-unity correlation because negation tokens are attenuated early in the text encoder, and a targeted text-side intervention can restore contrast.
method_sketch: Build positive-negated prompt pairs over common categories, compute patch similarity map correlations for three VLMs, then run layer-wise text-encoder interventions to find where negation signal dies.
novelty_hook: Negation failure is documented for retrieval; a patch-level characterization with a text-encoder localization study appears missing; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Negation may be represented but overridden at the joint-similarity stage, making text-encoder localization misleading.

title: Depth-wise division of labor between texture words and object nouns
one_line_idea: Test whether early VLM layers align patches with material and texture vocabulary while late layers align with object nouns, enabling prompt-dependent layer routing for dense tasks.
problem: Dense readouts use one fixed layer for all prompts, though linguistic categories plausibly align at different depths.
core_hypothesis: Alignment strength for texture and material words peaks earlier in the encoder than for object nouns, and routing each query to its best depth improves dense retrieval over any single-layer readout.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-word-class alignment-vs-depth curves show systematically earlier peaks for texture and material terms across models, and depth routing beats the best fixed layer; identical peak depths falsify the division of labor.
why_important: A vocabulary-conditioned readout would improve open-vocabulary dense tasks without retraining and refine our picture of what depth encodes in joint-embedding models.
why_possibly_novel: Depth-wise probing exists for pure vision models; a word-class-conditioned depth analysis of pixel-text alignment with a routing application appears new; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble texture-word and object-noun query sets with pixel ground truth (e.g. material and object segmentation datasets), sweep alignment per layer for two VLMs, then evaluate an oracle-free routing rule.
main_risk: Texture ground truth is scarce and noisy, and peak differences may be too small to exploit.
community_default_belief: The final aligned layer is where all text-relevant visual information concentrates.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Documented low-level feature specialization in early ViT layers should interact with the compositional structure of text, which no single-layer story captures.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Twenty texture words vs twenty object nouns on one material-segmentation dataset, per-layer alignment curves for one model, in a day.
core_claim: Alignment strength for texture and material words peaks earlier in the encoder than for object nouns, and routing each query to its best depth improves dense retrieval over any single-layer readout.
method_sketch: Assemble texture-word and object-noun query sets with pixel ground truth (e.g. material and object segmentation datasets), sweep alignment per layer for two VLMs, then evaluate an oracle-free routing rule.
novelty_hook: Depth-wise probing exists for pure vision models; a word-class-conditioned depth analysis of pixel-text alignment with a routing application appears new; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Texture ground truth is scarce and noisy, and peak differences may be too small to exploit.

title: Global-local consistency as a label-free dense capability score
one_line_idea: Test whether the agreement between a VLM's global image embedding and its aggregated patch embeddings predicts dense zero-shot performance across model checkpoints, giving a benchmark-free dense capability probe.
problem: Selecting a VLM checkpoint for dense tasks requires running segmentation benchmarks, which is slow and dataset-bound.
core_hypothesis: A single unlabeled-data statistic measuring global-local embedding consistency rank-correlates strongly with dense zero-shot mIoU across architectures and training recipes.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a pool of at least ten public VLM checkpoints, the consistency statistic achieves high rank correlation (predicting above 0.8 Spearman) with dense zero-shot mIoU; weak correlation falsifies the probe.
why_important: A cheap predictor would guide checkpoint selection and could serve as a training-time signal for dense-capable pretraining.
why_possibly_novel: Embedding-consistency statistics exist for other purposes; their use as a cross-model dense-capability predictor appears untested; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute the statistic on a few thousand unlabeled images for a checkpoint pool spanning CLIP variants and dense-oriented VLMs, then correlate with published-protocol dense zero-shot scores measured locally.
main_risk: The statistic may just track overall model quality, adding nothing over ImageNet accuracy as a predictor.
community_default_belief: Dense capability must be measured with dense benchmarks; no cheap unlabeled proxy exists.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense performance depends on properties (spatial coherence of alignment) that plausibly leave a strong signature in cheap statistics, as analogous proxies do for transferability prediction.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Five checkpoints, one dataset: compare proxy ranking with measured mIoU ranking; obvious disorder ends it within a day.
core_claim: A single unlabeled-data statistic measuring global-local embedding consistency rank-correlates strongly with dense zero-shot mIoU across architectures and training recipes.
method_sketch: Compute the statistic on a few thousand unlabeled images for a checkpoint pool spanning CLIP variants and dense-oriented VLMs, then correlate with published-protocol dense zero-shot scores measured locally.
novelty_hook: Embedding-consistency statistics exist for other purposes; their use as a cross-model dense-capability predictor appears untested; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: The statistic may just track overall model quality, adding nothing over ImageNet accuracy as a predictor.

title: Caption-scale ceiling for boundary quality
one_line_idea: Test whether scaling image-text pairs improves region-level open-vocab segmentation but leaves boundary-F1 flat, indicating boundaries need a different supervision channel than captions.
problem: Open-vocab segmentation pipelines assume that ever-larger caption corpora will keep improving dense quality, without separating region accuracy from boundary accuracy.
core_hypothesis: Caption supervision carries region-level semantics but essentially no boundary information, so boundary-F1 saturates early in caption-scale while region mIoU keeps rising.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a caption-scale sweep at fixed architecture, region mIoU rises monotonically while boundary-F1 plateaus at a small fraction of the region gains; parallel improvement of both falsifies the ceiling.
why_important: It would tell the field to stop paying for boundary quality with caption scale and to invest in cheap boundary-specific signals instead.
why_possibly_novel: Scale studies report aggregate mIoU; a boundary-decomposed scaling analysis for caption-supervised dense models seems unreported; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train or gather checkpoints of one caption-supervised segmentation method at three data scales, evaluate region mIoU and boundary-F1 separately on two benchmarks, and compare scaling slopes.
main_risk: Public checkpoints confound data scale with other recipe changes, requiring controlled retraining that is compute-heavy.
community_default_belief: More paired data lifts all aspects of dense performance together.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Captions almost never describe object boundaries, so the gradient signal for crisp edges must come from architectural priors that saturate, not from data volume.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Evaluate existing small-vs-large-data public checkpoints of one method family with boundary-F1; if boundary gains track region gains proportionally, the ceiling claim dies cheaply.
core_claim: Caption supervision carries region-level semantics but essentially no boundary information, so boundary-F1 saturates early in caption-scale while region mIoU keeps rising.
method_sketch: Train or gather checkpoints of one caption-supervised segmentation method at three data scales, evaluate region mIoU and boundary-F1 separately on two benchmarks, and compare scaling slopes.
novelty_hook: Scale studies report aggregate mIoU; a boundary-decomposed scaling analysis for caption-supervised dense models seems unreported; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Public checkpoints confound data scale with other recipe changes, requiring controlled retraining that is compute-heavy.

title: SAM pseudo-mask self-training imports part-whole bias
one_line_idea: Test whether open-vocab segmenters self-trained on SAM-generated pseudo-masks inherit SAM's characteristic over-segmentation of articulated objects, measurably shifting their part-whole granularity.
problem: Using SAM masks as free dense supervision is now routine, but the granularity prior of the mask generator is treated as neutral ground truth.
core_hypothesis: Students trained on SAM pseudo-masks show systematically higher part-level fragmentation on articulated categories (people, animals, vehicles) than caption-only or human-mask baselines, in proportion to pseudo-label exposure.
falsifiable_prediction: A fragmentation metric on articulated classes increases monotonically with the fraction of SAM pseudo-labels in training; no dose-response falsifies the inheritance claim.
why_important: Pseudo-mask pipelines are multiplying; knowing they transmit granularity bias would change how the community filters or reweights generated masks.
why_possibly_novel: Pseudo-label noise is studied generically; granularity-bias inheritance from promptable mask generators into VLM segmenters appears uncharacterized; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train the same open-vocab student with 0, 50, and 100 percent SAM pseudo-masks on a fixed image pool; measure per-class fragmentation and whole-object IoU on articulated vs rigid categories.
main_risk: Fragmentation differences may be small relative to training noise at affordable scales.
community_default_belief: SAM masks are high-quality class-agnostic supervision whose biases are negligible for downstream semantics.
why_it_might_be_wrong: SAM's prompt-conditioned granularity ambiguity is well known qualitatively, and students are known to copy teacher biases at scale in other domains.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compare fragmentation statistics of one public SAM-distilled model vs one caption-trained model on person and animal classes in a day; identical statistics undermine the claim.
core_claim: Students trained on SAM pseudo-masks show systematically higher part-level fragmentation on articulated categories (people, animals, vehicles) than caption-only or human-mask baselines, in proportion to pseudo-label exposure.
method_sketch: Train the same open-vocab student with 0, 50, and 100 percent SAM pseudo-masks on a fixed image pool; measure per-class fragmentation and whole-object IoU on articulated vs rigid categories.
novelty_hook: Pseudo-label noise is studied generically; granularity-bias inheritance from promptable mask generators into VLM segmenters appears uncharacterized; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Fragmentation differences may be small relative to training noise at affordable scales.

title: Grounding accuracy follows caption-corpus word frequency
one_line_idea: Test whether per-category dense grounding accuracy is predictable from the category name's frequency in the pretraining caption corpus, largely independent of architecture.
problem: Open-vocab models fail on rare categories, but there is no quantitative law linking text-corpus statistics to dense performance that would let practitioners predict failures in advance.
core_hypothesis: Log caption frequency of a category explains most of the variance in its dense grounding accuracy across models sharing a data distribution, with architecture shifting the curve but not its shape.
falsifiable_prediction: A frequency-to-accuracy regression fit on one model transfers to other models trained on similar corpora with high rank correlation; architecture-dependent curve shapes falsify the data-dominance claim.
why_important: A predictive frequency law would let deployers anticipate rare-class failures and quantify how much data curation buys versus architecture work.
why_possibly_novel: Frequency effects are shown for classification; a cross-model quantitative frequency law for dense grounding appears missing; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate category frequencies from an open caption corpus, evaluate per-class open-vocab segmentation for three models on a wide-vocabulary benchmark, and fit and cross-validate the regression.
main_risk: Visual difficulty confounds frequency, requiring careful controls (object size, count) that thin out the class sample.
community_default_belief: Rare-class failure is a general long-tail problem to be fixed by better architectures or losses.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If accuracy is essentially set by corpus statistics, architecture-side fixes are treating a symptom, which matches evidence from image-level tasks.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One model, one benchmark, frequencies from a public corpus: scatter and correlation in two days; a weak correlation ends the strong version of the law.
core_claim: Log caption frequency of a category explains most of the variance in its dense grounding accuracy across models sharing a data distribution, with architecture shifting the curve but not its shape.
method_sketch: Estimate category frequencies from an open caption corpus, evaluate per-class open-vocab segmentation for three models on a wide-vocabulary benchmark, and fit and cross-validate the regression.
novelty_hook: Frequency effects are shown for classification; a cross-model quantitative frequency law for dense grounding appears missing; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Visual difficulty confounds frequency, requiring careful controls (object size, count) that thin out the class sample.

title: Classification, not proposals, dominates open-vocab error
one_line_idea: Decompose two-stage open-vocabulary segmentation error into mask-proposal misses versus label-assignment mistakes and test whether label assignment dominates at current scale.
problem: The field invests in better class-agnostic proposal networks and better VLM classifiers simultaneously without a clear accounting of which failure dominates.
core_hypothesis: With oracle labels, current proposal sets already cover the large majority of ground-truth regions, so most residual error is misclassification of correctly proposed masks.
falsifiable_prediction: Oracle-label evaluation of proposal sets yields mIoU far above end-to-end performance (predicting a gap of tens of points), and the gap persists across datasets; a small oracle gap falsifies classification dominance.

title: Positional shortcut learning in patch-level contrastive objectives
one_line_idea: Test whether dense contrastive pretraining with intra-image negatives learns positional shortcuts, and whether spatially matched inter-image negatives remove them.

title: Nameability bias from MLLM-generated dense supervision
one_line_idea: Test whether training segmenters on MLLM-generated dense captions induces a bias where easily nameable objects get better masks, quantifiable and correctable with a nameability score.
problem: Synthetic dense captions from MLLMs are becoming standard supervision, but MLLMs describe nameable, prototypical objects more readily than awkward-to-name regions.

title: Dense alignment emerges abruptly during contrastive pretraining
one_line_idea: Sweep checkpoints across contrastive pretraining to test whether patch-level text alignment appears abruptly after a compute threshold rather than improving smoothly.
problem: Nobody knows when in pretraining dense alignment arises, so dense-capability planning (how much pretraining before dense fine-tuning) is guesswork.

title: Fine-tuning erodes attribute vocabulary before noun vocabulary
one_line_idea: Test whether dense fine-tuning on closed-vocabulary datasets erodes open-vocab alignment non-uniformly, hitting attribute and relation vocabulary harder than object nouns.
problem: Catastrophic vocabulary narrowing from dense fine-tuning is reported as a scalar, hiding which parts of language competence are lost first.
core_hypothesis: Because closed-vocab targets are noun-centric, gradient pressure preserves noun alignment while attribute and relation alignment decays fastest, in a consistent order across models.
falsifiable_prediction: Post-fine-tuning alignment drop, measured per word class on held-out dense probes, is significantly larger for attributes and relations than nouns across three models; uniform decay falsifies the ordered-erosion claim.
why_important: It would define what regularization must protect and provide a finer-grained metric for open-vocab retention than aggregate unseen-class mIoU.
why_possibly_novel: Forgetting in VLM fine-tuning is studied at class level; a word-class-resolved erosion analysis for dense models appears new; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune two open-vocab segmenters on COCO-style vocab, then evaluate attribute-conditioned and relation-conditioned dense retrieval probes before and after, alongside noun probes.

community_default_belief: Fine-tuning shrinks the effective vocabulary roughly uniformly toward the training classes.

title: Frozen text encoders silently narrow effective vocabulary
one_line_idea: Test whether freezing the text encoder during dense fine-tuning, a standard open-vocab-preserving trick, actually lets the image encoder drift toward exploiting text-space anisotropy, narrowing the effective vocabulary while headline unseen-class metrics look fine.
problem: Freezing the text tower is assumed to preserve open-vocabulary behavior, but preservation is only verified on small unseen-class sets.
core_hypothesis: Image features after fine-tuning align to a lower-dimensional subspace of text space concentrated around training-class directions, so performance on genuinely distant vocabulary drops even though nearby unseen classes survive.
falsifiable_prediction: Effective dimensionality of image-feature projections onto text space shrinks after fine-tuning, and accuracy on distant-vocabulary probes drops disproportionately versus near-vocabulary unseen classes; no such asymmetry falsifies the drift story.

title: Spatial prepositions in captions are load-bearing for dense alignment
one_line_idea: Ablate spatial language (prepositions and relational phrases) from pretraining captions and test whether dense alignment degrades much more than global retrieval, isolating the supervision value of spatial words.
problem: It is unknown which caption content teaches VLMs localization; the field scales all text equally.
core_hypothesis: A small fraction of caption tokens carrying spatial relations contributes disproportionately to patch-level alignment, so their removal selectively harms dense metrics while leaving global retrieval nearly intact.
falsifiable_prediction: Preposition-ablated pretraining loses several points of dense zero-shot mIoU but under one point of retrieval recall at matched scale; equal degradation falsifies the special role of spatial language.
why_important: It would identify which data to curate or synthesize for dense-capable pretraining instead of paying for undifferentiated scale.
why_possibly_novel: Caption ablations exist for attributes and objects at image level; a spatial-language ablation targeted at dense alignment appears untested; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain two small CLIP-style models on identical images with original vs spatial-language-stripped captions, evaluate global retrieval and dense zero-shot readout on standard benchmarks.
main_risk: Small-scale pretraining may under-represent the mechanism by which spatial words matter at production scale.

title: How much of referring segmentation is head-noun plus saliency
one_line_idea: Quantify the fraction of standard referring-segmentation benchmarks solvable by ignoring all relational content and using only the head noun with a saliency prior.
problem: Referring segmentation scores are read as evidence of relational language understanding, but many test items may be solvable without processing the relation at all.
core_hypothesis: A deliberately impoverished baseline (head-noun grounding plus generic saliency and size priors) solves a large share of RefCOCO-family items, and model-over-baseline margins are concentrated in a small hard subset.
falsifiable_prediction: The impoverished baseline reaches within a moderate gap of full models on overall IoU, and item-level analysis shows current SOTA gains come mostly from items the baseline also solves; a large uniform gap falsifies the shortcut account.

why_it_might_be_wrong: Dataset construction favored short discriminative expressions, and single-salient-object images make relations redundant for many items.

title: Negated referring expressions are at chance and scale does not help
one_line_idea: Construct a negation-controlled referring benchmark (the cup without a handle) and test whether accuracy is at chance and flat across model scale, indicating a supervision gap rather than a capacity gap.
problem: Negation in referring expressions is anecdotally broken, but there is no controlled measurement isolating negation from other difficulty, nor a scale analysis.
core_hypothesis: On minimal pairs differing only in a negated attribute, referring models perform near chance regardless of parameter count, and small amounts of explicit negative-pair supervision fix it where scale does not.
falsifiable_prediction: Accuracy on negation minimal pairs is statistically indistinguishable from chance across a model-size sweep, while a modest fine-tune on synthetic negation pairs lifts it strongly; smooth improvement with scale falsifies the supervision-gap account.
why_important: Exclusion queries are central to interactive segmentation and data curation tools, and the scale-vs-supervision question determines the fix.
why_possibly_novel: Negation failures are documented for retrieval; a minimal-pair dense benchmark with a scale sweep and a supervision-injection contrast appears new; novelty unverified.

community_default_belief: Language understanding failures of VLMs, including negation, improve steadily with scale.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Contrastive and grounding objectives provide almost no gradient that distinguishes negated from affirmative mentions, so no amount of scale changes the training signal.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Fifty hand-built negation pairs on one large and one small model in a day; if the large model is clearly above chance, the flat-scale claim dies.

title: Ordinal reference collapses under mirror flips
one_line_idea: Test whether referring models resolving ordinal and positional expressions (second from the left) rely on brittle absolute-position features that fail under horizontal mirroring, unlike human-robust relative encodings.
problem: Positional expressions require coordinate-frame reasoning, but models may fake it with absolute positional-embedding correlations that do not survive simple viewpoint transforms.
core_hypothesis: Accuracy on ordinal expressions drops far more under horizontal flip (with text left-right terms swapped accordingly) than accuracy on non-positional expressions, revealing absolute-position shortcut use.
falsifiable_prediction: The flip-consistency gap for positional items is several times the gap for non-positional items across models; equal gaps falsify the shortcut claim.
why_important: Robust spatial reference matters for robotics and AR instruction following, where camera mirroring and viewpoint changes are routine.
why_possibly_novel: Flip-consistency is a standard augmentation topic, but as a targeted probe of ordinal reference mechanisms in referring segmentation it appears unused; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Filter positional expressions from RefCOCO-family data, construct flipped image-text pairs with correctly swapped lateral terms, and measure paired accuracy for three models.
main_risk: Term-swapping requires careful linguistics (left of the man vs on the left), and errors there contaminate the probe.
community_default_belief: Models that score well on positional expressions have learned relative spatial reasoning.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Learned positional embeddings give a cheap absolute-coordinate cue that the training distribution never penalizes, and shortcut learning predicts models will prefer it.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One model, two hundred positional items, flip test in an afternoon; small asymmetry ends the strong claim.
core_claim: Accuracy on ordinal expressions drops far more under horizontal flip (with text left-right terms swapped accordingly) than accuracy on non-positional expressions, revealing absolute-position shortcut use.

novelty_hook: Flip-consistency is a standard augmentation topic, but as a targeted probe of ordinal reference mechanisms in referring segmentation it appears unused; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Term-swapping requires careful linguistics (left of the man vs on the left), and errors there contaminate the probe.

title: Single-target architectures systematically fragment plural referents
one_line_idea: Characterize how referring models trained under a one-expression-one-mask assumption fail on plural and group expressions, and test whether the failure is a decodable architecture artifact rather than a language gap.
problem: Most referring pipelines assume a single target mask, yet natural expressions frequently denote sets (the three dogs, all the red chairs).
core_hypothesis: On plural expressions, single-target models produce characteristic failure signatures (largest-instance-only or merged-fragment masks) predictable from their decoder structure, and set-aware decoding fixes them without new language supervision.
falsifiable_prediction: Failure-mode distribution on plural items differs sharply by decoder family (query-based vs per-pixel), and retrofitting a set decoder onto the same encoder closes most of the plural gap; uniform failure across decoders falsifies the architectural account.
why_important: Plural reference is ubiquitous in real instructions, and knowing the failure is architectural tells the field it is cheap to fix.
why_possibly_novel: Generalized referring datasets exist; a decoder-family-resolved failure taxonomy with a retrofit experiment appears new; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate three architecture families on a plural-rich referring set, categorize failures automatically by mask-instance analysis, then retrain only the decoder head of one model with set supervision.
main_risk: Retrofit gains may come from extra training rather than the decoder change, requiring careful compute matching.
community_default_belief: Plural referring failures reflect insufficient language understanding requiring better multimodal pretraining.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The single-mask output format makes correct plural behavior structurally impossible regardless of language competence, so the bottleneck sits after understanding.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Feed plural expressions to one model and inspect whether predicted masks cover single instances despite correct noun grounding, in a day.
core_claim: On plural expressions, single-target models produce characteristic failure signatures (largest-instance-only or merged-fragment masks) predictable from their decoder structure, and set-aware decoding fixes them without new language supervision.
method_sketch: Evaluate three architecture families on a plural-rich referring set, categorize failures automatically by mask-instance analysis, then retrain only the decoder head of one model with set supervision.
novelty_hook: Generalized referring datasets exist; a decoder-family-resolved failure taxonomy with a retrofit experiment appears new; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Retrofit gains may come from extra training rather than the decoder change, requiring careful compute matching.

title: Non-monotonic relationship between expression length and referring accuracy
one_line_idea: Test whether adding disambiguating detail to referring expressions helps up to a point and then hurts, because text-encoder dilution overwhelms the extra information.
problem: Users assume more descriptive expressions make referring easier, but pooled text representations may dilute the discriminative tokens as length grows.
core_hypothesis: Accuracy as a function of controlled expression length is inverted-U shaped for pooled-text-embedding models but monotonic for token-level cross-attention models, tying the effect to the text bottleneck.
falsifiable_prediction: Length-controlled evaluation shows a significant accuracy decline beyond a modest length for pooled models and no decline for token-level fusion models; monotonic curves for both falsify the dilution mechanism.
why_important: It gives practical prompt guidance for interactive tools and a concrete architectural criterion (token-level fusion) for referring systems.
why_possibly_novel: Length effects are folklore; a controlled same-referent length-manipulation study contrasting fusion mechanisms appears unreported; novelty unverified.

main_risk: Longer generated expressions may accidentally introduce new ambiguities or errors, confounding length with correctness.
community_default_belief: More information in the expression can only help or at worst saturate.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fixed-dimensional pooled text embeddings must trade off token contributions, so informative heads get diluted by additive detail, a mechanism absent only in token-level fusion.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Take one hundred referents, three lengths each, one pooled model: if accuracy at longest length is not below medium length, dilution is not biting.

method_sketch: Generate nested expressions of increasing length for the same referents (verified unambiguous at every length), evaluate two pooled-embedding and two cross-attention referring models across lengths.
novelty_hook: Length effects are folklore; a controlled same-referent length-manipulation study contrasting fusion mechanisms appears unreported; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Longer generated expressions may accidentally introduce new ambiguities or errors, confounding length with correctness.

title: Pragmatics mismatch between interactive-game data and exhaustive descriptions
one_line_idea: Test whether models trained on interactively collected referring data (pragmatically brief) systematically underperform on exhaustive-style descriptions and vice versa, revealing a hidden pragmatics domain gap.
problem: RefCOCO expressions come from a time-pressured two-player game and encode minimal-effort pragmatics, while deployed systems receive very different linguistic registers.
core_hypothesis: Cross-register evaluation (train on game-style, test on exhaustive-style and conversely) shows a substantial accuracy drop in both directions that persists after vocabulary matching, isolating pragmatics as a domain axis.
falsifiable_prediction: Cross-register drops exceed within-register test-retest differences by a clear margin on the same images and referents; negligible drops falsify pragmatics as a meaningful domain gap.

why_possibly_novel: Dataset bias in referring data is discussed; a controlled same-referent register-swap experiment appears missing; novelty unverified.

main_risk: Generated exhaustive descriptions may differ from human exhaustive style, weakening external validity.
community_default_belief: Referring data generalizes across phrasing styles since the underlying grounding task is the same.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Pragmatic brevity changes which features are mentioned at all (discriminative vs descriptive), so the input distributions differ semantically, not just stylistically.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Two hundred referents, model-generated exhaustive rewrites human-verified, one model, both directions, within three days.
core_claim: Cross-register evaluation (train on game-style, test on exhaustive-style and conversely) shows a substantial accuracy drop in both directions that persists after vocabulary matching, isolating pragmatics as a domain axis.
method_sketch: Collect or generate exhaustive descriptions for existing RefCOCO referents, verify referential success with humans, then run bidirectional cross-register evaluation with matched vocabulary statistics.
novelty_hook: Dataset bias in referring data is discussed; a controlled same-referent register-swap experiment appears missing; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Generated exhaustive descriptions may differ from human exhaustive style, weakening external validity.

title: Referring segmentation equals grounding plus class-agnostic masking
one_line_idea: Test whether a modular pipeline (phrase-grounded box then promptable mask) matches end-to-end pixel-text alignment models on current referring benchmarks, isolating where dense language alignment actually pays off.
problem: End-to-end referring architectures are assumed necessary, but the task may decompose cleanly into box-level grounding and language-free masking on existing benchmarks.
core_hypothesis: The modular pipeline matches end-to-end models on standard benchmarks, and the residual gap concentrates in items where the linguistic content constrains pixels directly (parts, amorphous regions, occlusion order).
falsifiable_prediction: Overall IoU difference between pipeline and end-to-end is small, while a curated pixel-linguistic subset shows a large end-to-end advantage; a large overall gap falsifies the decomposition claim.
why_important: It clarifies what end-to-end dense alignment buys and defines the item types future benchmarks need to reward it.
why_possibly_novel: Grounded-SAM-style pipelines are used in practice; a controlled decomposition study with a targeted residual analysis appears unpublished; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build the pipeline from a strong grounding detector and a promptable segmenter, evaluate against two end-to-end models on RefCOCO-family sets, and label residual-gap items by linguistic type.
main_risk: Pipeline performance depends heavily on the chosen components, making conclusions sensitive to component quality.
community_default_belief: Pixel-level language conditioning is required for referring segmentation, justifying end-to-end architectures.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Most benchmark referents are whole objects for which a correct box determines the mask, so the language never needs to touch pixels.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Assemble the pipeline from public checkpoints and run RefCOCO val in two days; a large deficit ends the claim.
core_claim: The modular pipeline matches end-to-end models on standard benchmarks, and the residual gap concentrates in items where the linguistic content constrains pixels directly (parts, amorphous regions, occlusion order).
method_sketch: Build the pipeline from a strong grounding detector and a promptable segmenter, evaluate against two end-to-end models on RefCOCO-family sets, and label residual-gap items by linguistic type.
novelty_hook: Grounded-SAM-style pipelines are used in practice; a controlled decomposition study with a targeted residual analysis appears unpublished; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Pipeline performance depends heavily on the chosen components, making conclusions sensitive to component quality.

title: Verb grounding in referring expressions is co-occurrence, not relation reading
one_line_idea: Use object-swap counterfactuals to test whether models resolve verb-mediated expressions (the man holding the racket) via object co-occurrence statistics rather than actually verifying the interaction.
problem: High accuracy on verb-containing expressions is taken as interaction understanding, but co-occurrence of the mentioned object may suffice on natural images.
core_hypothesis: On counterfactual scenes where the named object is present but the interaction does not hold (racket lying beside a different man), models select the co-occurrence match at high rates, revealing shortcut resolution.
falsifiable_prediction: Counterfactual accuracy drops to near chance while normal-scene accuracy stays high for the same expression templates; preserved counterfactual accuracy falsifies the shortcut claim.
why_important: Interaction-sensitive reference matters for embodied instruction following where several agents and objects co-occur.
why_possibly_novel: Counterfactual probing exists for VQA verbs; a segmentation-level object-swap protocol for referring expressions appears new; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate or composite images with interaction-broken counterfactuals, run three referring models on matched expression sets, and compare normal vs counterfactual selection rates.
main_risk: Composited counterfactuals introduce artifacts that models may detect, requiring a real-photo subset for validation.
community_default_belief: Verb-phrase referring accuracy demonstrates learned human-object interaction understanding.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Benchmark scenes rarely include the distractor configuration that would expose co-occurrence shortcuts, so the training signal never separates the strategies.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Fifty manually curated interaction-broken photos from existing HOI datasets, one model, one day.
core_claim: On counterfactual scenes where the named object is present but the interaction does not hold (racket lying beside a different man), models select the co-occurrence match at high rates, revealing shortcut resolution.
method_sketch: Curate or composite images with interaction-broken counterfactuals, run three referring models on matched expression sets, and compare normal vs counterfactual selection rates.
novelty_hook: Counterfactual probing exists for VQA verbs; a segmentation-level object-swap protocol for referring expressions appears new; novelty unverified.
