title: Cross-lingual referring degradation is mostly tokenization, not semantics
one_line_idea: Decompose the performance drop of multilingual referring segmentation into tokenization-induced text-encoder degradation versus genuine semantic transfer failure.
problem: Referring models degrade on non-English expressions, and the community attributes this to data scarcity without separating a mundane cause: tokenizers fragmenting non-English words into low-quality pieces.
core_hypothesis: Controlling semantic content via parallel expressions, the drop correlates strongly with tokenization fragmentation rate per language, and vocabulary-adapted re-tokenization recovers a large share without any new grounding data.
falsifiable_prediction: Fragmentation statistics predict per-language accuracy drops with high correlation, and tokenizer adaptation alone recovers a majority of the gap for high-fragmentation languages; weak correlation falsifies the tokenization account.
why_important: It would redirect multilingual grounding work from expensive data collection toward cheap tokenizer and embedding fixes where those suffice.
why_possibly_novel: Tokenization effects are studied in multilingual NLP; their causal isolation for dense grounding tasks appears missing; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build parallel referring expressions in five languages for the same referents, measure accuracy and fragmentation per language, then apply embedding-space tokenizer adaptation to one model and re-measure.
main_risk: Parallel translations can shift pragmatics and difficulty, contaminating the language comparison.
community_default_belief: Multilingual grounding gaps reflect missing multilingual paired data and require multilingual pretraining to fix.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The grounding happens in a shared embedding space; if text embeddings for fragmented words are simply noisy, the failure is upstream of grounding entirely.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Two languages with very different fragmentation rates, matched expressions, one model, two days; equal drops despite unequal fragmentation kills the account.
core_claim: Controlling semantic content via parallel expressions, the drop correlates strongly with tokenization fragmentation rate per language, and vocabulary-adapted re-tokenization recovers a large share without any new grounding data.
method_sketch: Build parallel referring expressions in five languages for the same referents, measure accuracy and fragmentation per language, then apply embedding-space tokenizer adaptation to one model and re-measure.
novelty_hook: Tokenization effects are studied in multilingual NLP; their causal isolation for dense grounding tasks appears missing; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Parallel translations can shift pragmatics and difficulty, contaminating the language comparison.

title: Exclusion memory beats re-prompting for interactive referring repair
one_line_idea: Test whether a simple candidate-mask exclusion memory handles conversational repair (no, the other one) better than feeding the full corrected dialogue back through an end-to-end referring model.
problem: Interactive referring systems must handle corrections, but current models are stateless and re-prompting with appended corrections may not implement exclusion at all.
core_hypothesis: End-to-end models ignore or misuse correction turns (predicting the same region again at high rates), while an explicit mechanism that removes rejected candidates and re-ranks achieves much higher repair success without retraining.
falsifiable_prediction: Repeat-prediction rate after a rejection stays high for dialogue re-prompting but near zero for exclusion memory, with higher final accuracy; comparable repair success for re-prompting falsifies the statelessness claim.
why_important: Repair is the most common real interaction pattern, and a training-free structural fix would immediately improve deployed annotation and AR tools.
why_possibly_novel: Interactive segmentation studies clicks; structured linguistic repair with exclusion semantics over candidate sets appears understudied; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate repair dialogues on ambiguous referents from generalized referring data, compare re-prompting vs exclusion-memory wrappers around the same base model, measure repair success and turns-to-success.
main_risk: Simulated rejections may not match human correction language, limiting external validity.
community_default_belief: Scaling instruction-tuned multimodal models will handle dialogue corrections implicitly, no explicit state needed.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Exclusion is a hard set-operation constraint; soft attention over a correction phrase does not implement it, and no training data teaches it.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One hundred two-turn repair episodes on one model with both wrappers, two days including harness construction.
core_claim: End-to-end models ignore or misuse correction turns (predicting the same region again at high rates), while an explicit mechanism that removes rejected candidates and re-ranks achieves much higher repair success without retraining.
method_sketch: Simulate repair dialogues on ambiguous referents from generalized referring data, compare re-prompting vs exclusion-memory wrappers around the same base model, measure repair success and turns-to-success.
novelty_hook: Interactive segmentation studies clicks; structured linguistic repair with exclusion semantics over candidate sets appears understudied; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Simulated rejections may not match human correction language, limiting external validity.

title: Absent-referent false positives are predictable from text neighborhood density
one_line_idea: Test whether the rate at which grounding models hallucinate boxes or masks for absent categories is predictable from the density of the category's neighborhood in text embedding space.
problem: Open-vocabulary grounding models produce confident detections for objects that are not in the image, and there is no predictive account of which prompts trigger this.
core_hypothesis: Categories whose text embeddings sit in dense neighborhoods (many similar concepts) hallucinate more because near-miss visual evidence is misattributed, making false-positive rate a function of text-space geometry.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a large absent-category evaluation, neighborhood density explains substantial variance in false-positive rate after controlling for frequency; no relationship falsifies the geometric account.
why_important: A predictive hallucination model enables prompt-level risk scoring in deployment without any image processing.
why_possibly_novel: Object hallucination is studied for captioning; a text-geometry predictive model for dense grounding false positives appears new; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For two grounding models, query hundreds of absent categories on images with exhaustive annotations, regress false-positive rates on embedding-neighborhood statistics and corpus frequency.
main_risk: Exhaustive absence ground truth is only approximate, and unannotated true positives corrupt the false-positive signal.
community_default_belief: Grounding hallucination is a miscalibration issue to be fixed with better confidence thresholds.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Thresholds cannot fix errors whose scores are systematically inflated by embedding-space crowding; the failure would be structural, not calibrational.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Fifty absent categories spanning sparse and dense text neighborhoods on one model in a day; no rate difference undermines the account.
core_claim: Categories whose text embeddings sit in dense neighborhoods (many similar concepts) hallucinate more because near-miss visual evidence is misattributed, making false-positive rate a function of text-space geometry.
method_sketch: For two grounding models, query hundreds of absent categories on images with exhaustive annotations, regress false-positive rates on embedding-neighborhood statistics and corpus frequency.
novelty_hook: Object hallucination is studied for captioning; a text-geometry predictive model for dense grounding false positives appears new; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Exhaustive absence ground truth is only approximate, and unannotated true positives corrupt the false-positive signal.

title: A vocabulary-size scaling law for grounding confidence calibration
one_line_idea: Characterize how detection confidence calibration of open-vocab grounding models shifts as distractor vocabulary grows, and fit a correction usable at any vocabulary size.
problem: Confidence scores of open-vocab detectors depend on the prompt vocabulary they are run with, but calibration is only ever measured at one vocabulary size.
core_hypothesis: Calibration error grows systematically and predictably with vocabulary size following a simple functional form, enabling a vocabulary-size-conditioned recalibration that transfers across datasets.
falsifiable_prediction: Fitted calibration-vs-vocabulary curves transfer across datasets within a small error, and the conditioned recalibration beats fixed-temperature baselines at all sizes; erratic non-transferable curves falsify the law.
why_important: Deployments constantly change their query vocabularies, and a transferable correction would make confidence thresholds meaningful again.
why_possibly_novel: Calibration of detectors is studied; vocabulary-size as an explicit calibration variable with a fitted law appears unexamined; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate two grounding models on two exhaustively annotated datasets under nested vocabularies from 10 to several thousand terms, fit calibration curves, and cross-validate the correction.
main_risk: Calibration may depend on which words are added, not how many, making size alone a weak variable.
community_default_belief: Per-dataset temperature scaling suffices for detector calibration.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Softmax-style competition among text queries mechanically changes score distributions with vocabulary size, an effect temperature fitted at one size cannot track.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One model, one dataset, five vocabulary sizes, calibration curves in a day; no monotone trend kills the law.
core_claim: Calibration error grows systematically and predictably with vocabulary size following a simple functional form, enabling a vocabulary-size-conditioned recalibration that transfers across datasets.
method_sketch: Evaluate two grounding models on two exhaustively annotated datasets under nested vocabularies from 10 to several thousand terms, fit calibration curves, and cross-validate the correction.
novelty_hook: Calibration of detectors is studied; vocabulary-size as an explicit calibration variable with a fitted law appears unexamined; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Calibration may depend on which words are added, not how many, making size alone a weak variable.

title: Word-order invariance exposes bag-of-words grounding
one_line_idea: Swap subject and object in relational grounding phrases (the dog on the sofa vs the sofa on the dog obviously reversed) and measure whether grounding outputs change appropriately, quantifying bag-of-words behavior at the dense level.
problem: Compositional insensitivity of VLMs is documented at image-caption level, but its dense-grounding footprint (which pixels get selected under role reversal) is unquantified.
core_hypothesis: Grounding models select nearly identical regions for role-reversed phrases, and the degree of invariance predicts their failures on relation-critical referring items, linking a cheap text perturbation to expensive relational evaluation.
falsifiable_prediction: Region-selection overlap between reversed pairs is high (predicting above 0.8 IoU of outputs) for contrastively trained grounding models, and per-model invariance rank-correlates with relational benchmark deficits; low overlap falsifies dense bag-of-words behavior.
why_important: A cheap invariance probe that predicts relational competence would let practitioners screen models without curated relational benchmarks.
why_possibly_novel: Word-order probes exist for retrieval; connecting dense output invariance to downstream relational performance appears new; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct role-reversible phrase pairs over images containing both entities, measure output-mask IoU between reversals for four models, correlate with their scores on relation-heavy referring subsets.
main_risk: Reversed phrases are often pragmatically anomalous, and models may fail them for reasons other than role encoding.
community_default_belief: Grounding models that localize both entities correctly are using the relation to pick the right one.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The training objective rewards lexical matching; syntax contributes little gradient, so role information is plausibly discarded.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One hundred reversible pairs, one model, output IoU histogram in an afternoon.
core_claim: Grounding models select nearly identical regions for role-reversed phrases, and the degree of invariance predicts their failures on relation-critical referring items, linking a cheap text perturbation to expensive relational evaluation.
method_sketch: Construct role-reversible phrase pairs over images containing both entities, measure output-mask IoU between reversals for four models, correlate with their scores on relation-heavy referring subsets.
novelty_hook: Word-order probes exist for retrieval; connecting dense output invariance to downstream relational performance appears new; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Reversed phrases are often pragmatically anomalous, and models may fail them for reasons other than role encoding.

title: Small-object grounding penalty exceeds the class-conditioned baseline
one_line_idea: Test whether text-conditioned detectors and segmenters suffer a systematically larger small-object penalty than class-conditioned counterparts at matched backbone resolution, implicating the text-conditioning pathway.
problem: Small-object weakness is universal in detection, but whether language conditioning adds an extra penalty on top of resolution limits is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Cross-modal attention pools evidence at a coarser effective granularity than class-conditioned heads, so the size-performance curve of text-conditioned models falls off faster below a size threshold at matched settings.
falsifiable_prediction: Size-stratified comparison at matched backbones and input resolutions shows a significantly steeper small-object decline for text-conditioned heads; identical curves falsify the extra-penalty claim.
why_important: It would identify a hidden cost of language conditioning and motivate granularity-aware fusion designs for surveillance, aerial, and document domains.
why_possibly_novel: Size stratification is routine; a controlled text-vs-class conditioning comparison isolating the fusion pathway appears missing; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train or obtain paired models sharing a backbone (one text-conditioned, one closed-vocab head), evaluate size-stratified AP and mIoU on the same datasets, compare decline slopes.
main_risk: Truly matched pairs are rare, and retraining both variants controls is compute-costly.
community_default_belief: Small-object failure is a resolution and FPN problem, orthogonal to how classes are specified.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Text-guided attention operates over patch tokens whose granularity bounds what a language query can select, an interaction absent in class-conditioned heads.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compare size-stratified curves of one open-vocab and one closed-vocab model with the same declared backbone on one dataset in a day; identical slopes weaken the claim.
core_claim: Cross-modal attention pools evidence at a coarser effective granularity than class-conditioned heads, so the size-performance curve of text-conditioned models falls off faster below a size threshold at matched settings.
method_sketch: Train or obtain paired models sharing a backbone (one text-conditioned, one closed-vocab head), evaluate size-stratified AP and mIoU on the same datasets, compare decline slopes.
novelty_hook: Size stratification is routine; a controlled text-vs-class conditioning comparison isolating the fusion pathway appears missing; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Truly matched pairs are rare, and retraining both variants controls is compute-costly.

title: Prompt templates tuned for classification are misfit for dense tasks
one_line_idea: Test whether the standard photo-of prompt templates inherited from image classification are systematically suboptimal for dense prediction, and whether dense-task-specific template search yields orthogonal gains across methods.
problem: Dense VLM pipelines reuse classification prompt templates without asking whether dense similarity readouts prefer different text statistics.
core_hypothesis: Optimal templates for dense readout differ consistently from classification-optimal ones (favoring region-level and material-level phrasing), and the gains from dense-specific templates stack with method-level improvements.
falsifiable_prediction: Template search on a dense validation task transfers gains of a consistent magnitude to unseen dense datasets and methods, while classification-optimal templates underperform; no transferable difference falsifies dense-template specificity.
why_important: Templates are free at deployment; consistent dense-specific gains would be immediately usable and would flag prompt choice as an uncontrolled variable in dense VLM papers.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt engineering for classification is heavily mined; systematic dense-task template characterization appears sparse; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run template search over a large template pool on one dense dataset, evaluate transfer to three other dense datasets and two readout methods against classification templates.
main_risk: Gains may be small relative to seed noise in dense metrics, requiring many evaluation repetitions.
community_default_belief: Ensembling standard templates suffices, and prompt effects are second-order for dense tasks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense readouts score every patch against text, so text statistics interact with patch statistics differently than with pooled image embeddings, plausibly shifting the optimum.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Fifty templates, one model, one dense dataset in a day; no meaningful spread across templates ends the idea.
core_claim: Optimal templates for dense readout differ consistently from classification-optimal ones (favoring region-level and material-level phrasing), and the gains from dense-specific templates stack with method-level improvements.
method_sketch: Run template search over a large template pool on one dense dataset, evaluate transfer to three other dense datasets and two readout methods against classification templates.
novelty_hook: Prompt engineering for classification is heavily mined; systematic dense-task template characterization appears sparse; novelty unverified.

title: Duplicate-driven inflation of grounding benchmark scores
one_line_idea: Audit dense grounding benchmarks for near-duplicates of pretraining images in web-scale corpora and quantify how much reported accuracy is inflated by memorized instances.
problem: Web-pretrained grounding models are evaluated on benchmarks whose images circulate on the web, and dense tasks have not received the contamination audits that classification benchmarks have.
core_hypothesis: A measurable fraction of grounding benchmark images have near-duplicates in common pretraining corpora, and model accuracy on duplicated items is significantly higher, with the gap largest for rare-vocabulary items.
falsifiable_prediction: Duplicate-stratified evaluation shows a significant accuracy gap on rare categories; a negligible gap falsifies contamination as a meaningful inflator for dense tasks.
why_important: It calibrates trust in reported open-vocab numbers and establishes an audit protocol dense benchmarks currently lack.
why_possibly_novel: Contamination audits exist for classification and retrieval; dense grounding audits with rarity stratification appear absent; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run perceptual-hash and embedding-based duplicate detection between one open pretraining corpus and two grounding benchmarks, then compare per-item accuracy across duplicate strata for two models.
main_risk: Only some pretraining corpora are open, so results bound but do not settle contamination for proprietary models.
community_default_belief: Dense task structure (localization) makes memorization-based inflation negligible.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Memorizing an image-text pair can directly supply the referent identity and rough location, which is most of the answer for single-salient-object items.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Duplicate detection between LAION subsets and RefCOCO images plus stratified scoring of one model, feasible in three days.
core_claim: A measurable fraction of grounding benchmark images have near-duplicates in common pretraining corpora, and model accuracy on duplicated items is significantly higher, with the gap largest for rare-vocabulary items.
method_sketch: Run perceptual-hash and embedding-based duplicate detection between one open pretraining corpus and two grounding benchmarks, then compare per-item accuracy across duplicate strata for two models.
novelty_hook: Contamination audits exist for classification and retrieval; dense grounding audits with rarity stratification appear absent; novelty unverified.

title: A universal attribute-grounding difficulty ordering
one_line_idea: Test whether attribute grounding difficulty follows a stable ordering (color easiest, then material, then size, then relational attributes) across architectures and training recipes, indicating a data-driven rather than architecture-driven limit.
problem: Attribute grounding failures are reported anecdotally per model, with no test of whether the difficulty structure is model-independent.
core_hypothesis: The difficulty ordering over attribute types is invariant across diverse models because it reflects caption-data statistics and attribute verifiability, so architecture changes shuffle absolute scores but not the ordering.
falsifiable_prediction: Rank correlation of per-attribute-type accuracy across at least six models is very high; frequent order inversions across models falsify the universality claim.
why_important: A universal ordering would pinpoint supervision gaps as the binding constraint and argue against architecture-centric fixes for attribute grounding.
why_possibly_novel: Attribute benchmarks exist; a cross-model invariance analysis of difficulty structure appears unreported; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble attribute-typed dense grounding probes from existing attribute datasets, evaluate a diverse model pool, compute cross-model rank correlations of type-level accuracy.
main_risk: Attribute type taxonomies are contestable and probe difficulty may be unbalanced across types.
community_default_belief: Attribute grounding weaknesses are model-specific and addressable by architectural innovation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If all models drink from similar web data, their attribute competence should inherit the same statistical skeleton, as seen in other bias inheritances.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Three models on an existing attribute-grounding benchmark, type-level rank correlation in two days.
core_claim: The difficulty ordering over attribute types is invariant across diverse models because it reflects caption-data statistics and attribute verifiability, so architecture changes shuffle absolute scores but not the ordering.
method_sketch: Assemble attribute-typed dense grounding probes from existing attribute datasets, evaluate a diverse model pool, compute cross-model rank correlations of type-level accuracy.
novelty_hook: Attribute benchmarks exist; a cross-model invariance analysis of difficulty structure appears unreported; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Attribute type taxonomies are contestable and probe difficulty may be unbalanced across types.

title: Gradient conflict between category detection and referring objectives
one_line_idea: Measure whether joint training on category-level detection and expression-level referring creates gradient conflict that degrades relational sensitivity, explaining why joint models underperform specialists on relation-critical items.
problem: Unified grounding models train category and referring objectives together, assuming synergy, but the objectives may pull shared parameters in opposing directions on relational content.
core_hypothesis: Category-detection gradients dominate and suppress relation-encoding directions in shared layers, measurable as gradient cosine conflict that grows in layers where relational information is processed, and mitigable by gradient surgery.
falsifiable_prediction: Layer-wise gradient conflict correlates with relational-item degradation under joint training, and conflict-mitigation recovers most of the specialist gap; absence of conflict-degradation correlation falsifies the account.
why_important: Unified perception models are the current trend, and knowing where objectives fight would guide capacity allocation and loss scheduling.
why_possibly_novel: Gradient conflict is studied in multi-task learning broadly; its application to the category-vs-referring split with relational-item stratification appears new; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a mid-size grounding model jointly and separately, log layer-wise gradient cosines between objectives, evaluate relational-item subsets, and test one gradient-surgery intervention.
main_risk: Gradient cosine is a noisy proxy for functional interference, and conclusions may not survive scale changes.
community_default_belief: Category and referring supervision are mutually reinforcing forms of grounding.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Category supervision explicitly rewards ignoring context (detect all instances), while referring rewards context-dependence; on shared parameters those are opposing pressures.

core_claim: Category-detection gradients dominate and suppress relation-encoding directions in shared layers, measurable as gradient cosine conflict that grows in layers where relational information is processed, and mitigable by gradient surgery.
method_sketch: Train a mid-size grounding model jointly and separately, log layer-wise gradient cosines between objectives, evaluate relational-item subsets, and test one gradient-surgery intervention.
novelty_hook: Gradient conflict is studied in multi-task learning broadly; its application to the category-vs-referring split with relational-item stratification appears new; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Gradient cosine is a noisy proxy for functional interference, and conclusions may not survive scale changes.

title: Fusion depth should be conditioned on language type
one_line_idea: Test whether early text-vision fusion beats late fusion only for relational language, motivating an input-conditioned fusion-depth switch instead of a fixed design choice.
problem: The early-vs-late fusion debate for dense VLMs is argued with aggregate benchmarks that average over linguistically heterogeneous queries.
core_hypothesis: Language whose truth conditions bind image regions to each other (relations, comparatives) benefits from early fusion, while categorical queries are served equally well by late fusion, so the aggregate debate is ill-posed.
falsifiable_prediction: Stratifying evaluation by language type shows a fusion-depth interaction effect several times larger than the aggregate difference; no interaction falsifies language-conditioned fusion.
why_important: It would resolve a persistent architecture debate by dissolving it, and yield a cheap router that picks fusion depth per query.
why_possibly_novel: Fusion-depth ablations exist; a language-type-stratified interaction analysis with a routing consequence appears new; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched early-fusion and late-fusion referring models on identical data, evaluate on language-typed query subsets, test the interaction statistically, then prototype a query router.
main_risk: Language-type annotation is noisy and confounded with visual difficulty, requiring careful subset construction.
community_default_belief: One fusion depth is globally better, and the field should converge on it.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The computational role of fusion differs by query semantics: relations need vision-side computation to be text-steered, categories only need a final comparison.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Evaluate two public models known to differ in fusion depth on relation-heavy vs category-heavy referring subsets in a day; no differential pattern weakens the claim.

title: Instance-count degradation curve of single seg-token bottlenecks
one_line_idea: Characterize how mask quality of MLLM segmenters that compress the referent into one seg-token degrades with scene instance count, and test multi-token decoding as the fix.
problem: LISA-style architectures route all pixel-level intent through one embedding, an information bottleneck whose capacity limits are uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: Mask quality falls predictably as same-category instance count grows because one token cannot encode which-instance information robustly, and allocating multiple seg-tokens restores performance with sub-linear cost.
falsifiable_prediction: IoU-vs-instance-count curves show significantly steeper decline for single-token models than for multi-query baselines at matched training, and multi-token retrofits flatten the curve; parallel curves falsify the bottleneck account.
why_important: Seg-token interfaces are proliferating in MLLMs, and knowing their structural capacity limit guides interface design before the pattern ossifies.
why_possibly_novel: Seg-token architectures are new enough that systematic bottleneck characterization appears absent; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate two seg-token models and one query-based baseline on instance-count-stratified referring data, then retrain one seg-token model with k tokens and re-measure the curve.
main_risk: Instance count correlates with clutter and occlusion, requiring covariate control to isolate the bottleneck.
community_default_belief: A single learned seg-token is a sufficient interface between language reasoning and mask decoding.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fixed-dimensional embeddings must trade off instance-identity precision against semantic content as scenes grow complex; the arithmetic is unforgiving.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Stratify existing benchmark results of one public seg-token model by instance count in an afternoon; a flat curve kills the bottleneck story.
core_claim: Mask quality falls predictably as same-category instance count grows because one token cannot encode which-instance information robustly, and allocating multiple seg-tokens restores performance with sub-linear cost.
method_sketch: Evaluate two seg-token models and one query-based baseline on instance-count-stratified referring data, then retrain one seg-token model with k tokens and re-measure the curve.
novelty_hook: Seg-token architectures are new enough that systematic bottleneck characterization appears absent; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Instance count correlates with clutter and occlusion, requiring covariate control to isolate the bottleneck.

title: The LLM in MLLM segmenters is mostly an expression parser
one_line_idea: Test whether the large language model inside MLLM-based segmentation contributes reasoning beyond expression parsing, by swapping it for a small text encoder and measuring where quality actually drops.
problem: MLLM segmenters carry billions of language parameters whose contribution to mask quality is unmeasured; they may pay only for parsing that a small model does equally well.
core_hypothesis: For non-inferential expressions, replacing the LLM with a compact encoder loses almost nothing, and the LLM advantage concentrates exclusively on items requiring world knowledge or multi-step inference.
falsifiable_prediction: A parameter-matched-interface swap shows near-zero loss on standard referring sets but a large loss on reasoning-segmentation items; uniform loss across item types falsifies the parser-only account.
why_important: It would let deployments serve most traffic with a small model and route only inferential queries to the LLM, cutting cost dramatically.
why_possibly_novel: Ablating the LLM out of segmentation MLLMs with item-type stratification appears undone; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take one open MLLM segmenter, retrain its projection with a small text encoder replacing the LLM at fixed decoder, evaluate on standard vs reasoning-typed subsets.
main_risk: Retraining the interface may under-utilize the small encoder, overstating the LLM advantage.
community_default_belief: End-to-end LLM integration is what enables high-quality language-driven segmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Most benchmark expressions are syntactically simple noun phrases whose grounding needs no inference, so the LLM may be idle capacity on the bulk of the distribution.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Route benchmark items through an LLM-paraphrase-to-simple-phrase pipeline feeding a small referring model; if that matches the MLLM on standard sets in two days of work, the parser account gains strong support.

title: Encoder conditioning vs decoder conditioning is a relation-dependence split
one_line_idea: Test whether injecting text into the visual encoder (rather than only the mask decoder) matters exclusively for queries whose resolution requires re-grouping visual features, using matched-capacity conditioning variants.

title: Visual token count, not image resolution, bounds dense VLM performance
one_line_idea: Disentangle token count from input resolution in dense VLMs to test whether performance is governed by the token budget almost regardless of the underlying pixel resolution.

title: Query competition priors from Mask2Former harm co-referent regions
one_line_idea: Test whether mask decoders inherited from query-competition architectures suppress secondary regions that language queries should include, causing systematic under-segmentation of co-referent sets.

title: Learnable dense prompt tokens converge to spatial anchors
one_line_idea: Probe whether learnable prompt or query tokens in dense VLMs converge to fixed spatial position detectors rather than semantic detectors, explaining both their efficiency and their center-bias failures.

title: One pyramid level carries almost all text-alignment signal

title: Top-k word routing preserves dense cross-attention quality except on function words
one_line_idea: Test whether pixel-word cross-attention can be sparsified to a few words per pixel with negligible loss, and characterize the predicted failure mode on function words that carry compositional load.

one_line_idea: Test whether MLLMs that emit box or polygon coordinates as text exhibit systematic snap-to-grid artifacts traceable to numeric tokenization, measurable in coordinate histograms and fixable with digit-level decoding constraints.

why_possibly_novel: Token pruning is popular; its linguistic failure characterization appears absent; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement standard text-conditioned pruning in one referring model, evaluate affirmative vs exclusion query sets across pruning ratios, map collapse thresholds.
main_risk: Exclusion queries are already weak unpruned, compressing the measurable gap.
community_default_belief: Text-guided pruning is safe because irrelevant tokens do not affect the answer.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For exclusion semantics the answer is constituted by the irrelevant tokens; relevance-based compression is semantically inverted for that query class.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Prune at seventy percent and compare affirmative vs negation accuracy on one model in a day.
core_claim: Similarity-based pruning preserves accuracy on affirmative queries at high pruning ratios but collapses on negation, universal quantification, and absence verification, because those require evidence from low-similarity tokens.
method_sketch: Implement standard text-conditioned pruning in one referring model, evaluate affirmative vs exclusion query sets across pruning ratios, map collapse thresholds.
novelty_hook: Token pruning is popular; its linguistic failure characterization appears absent; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Exclusion queries are already weak unpruned, compressing the measurable gap.

title: Dense alignment distills with far less data than it took to learn
one_line_idea: Test whether pixel-text alignment can be distilled from large VLMs into small ones using orders of magnitude less data than original training, because alignment structure is low-rank relative to representation learning.
problem: Small deployable models lack dense language alignment, and the assumed fix (training small models on web-scale data) is expensive; distillation data requirements for the alignment component specifically are unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: Given a strong self-supervised small backbone, aligning it to a teacher's pixel-text space needs only a modest unlabeled image set, with distillation quality saturating early, because the transferred object is a map between spaces, not the spaces themselves.
falsifiable_prediction: Distillation-data scaling curves saturate at a small fraction of teacher training data (predicting under one percent) for dense zero-shot transfer; slow saturation falsifies the low-rank-transfer account.
why_important: Cheap alignment distillation would put open-vocab dense capability on edge devices without web-scale training runs.
why_possibly_novel: VLM distillation exists; the data-requirement scaling analysis specific to dense alignment transfer appears missing; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Distill patch-text alignment from one large VLM into a small self-supervised backbone across a data-size sweep, evaluate dense zero-shot per size, fit the saturation curve.
main_risk: Teacher-specific artifacts may transfer with the alignment, capping student quality below usefulness.
community_default_belief: Dense open-vocab capability requires large-scale paired training, even for distillation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If the student already has good visual structure, alignment is a low-dimensional re-basing that small data can pin down, unlike representation learning proper.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Distill on one hundred thousand images and evaluate dense zero-shot in three days; a huge gap to the teacher weakens the claim.
core_claim: Given a strong self-supervised small backbone, aligning it to a teacher's pixel-text space needs only a modest unlabeled image set, with distillation quality saturating early, because the transferred object is a map between spaces, not the spaces themselves.
method_sketch: Distill patch-text alignment from one large VLM into a small self-supervised backbone across a data-size sweep, evaluate dense zero-shot per size, fit the saturation curve.
novelty_hook: VLM distillation exists; the data-requirement scaling analysis specific to dense alignment transfer appears missing; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Teacher-specific artifacts may transfer with the alignment, capping student quality below usefulness.

title: Quantization degrades spatial alignment before global recognition
one_line_idea: Test whether low-bit quantization of VLMs harms dense grounding at bitwidths where global classification is still intact, exposing a dense-specific deployment cliff current quantization benchmarks miss.
problem: Quantization decisions are validated on classification and retrieval metrics, and dense grounding quality is assumed to follow, without measurement.
core_hypothesis: Fine-grained spatial alignment depends on small activation differences that quantization noise destroys earlier than class-level margins, so dense metrics fall off one to two bits before global metrics across models and schemes.
falsifiable_prediction: Bitwidth sweeps show dense zero-shot degradation onset at systematically higher bitwidths than classification degradation, consistent across two quantization schemes; synchronized degradation falsifies the dense-first cliff.
why_important: Edge deployments choose bitwidths from global benchmarks and would silently ship broken grounding if the cliff is real.
why_possibly_novel: Quantization robustness is well studied for classification; task-granularity-stratified analysis for dense VLM outputs appears sparse; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Quantize two VLMs at four bitwidths under two schemes, evaluate classification, retrieval, and dense zero-shot metrics, compare degradation onsets.
main_risk: Results may be scheme-specific, requiring more schemes than budgeted to generalize.
community_default_belief: A quantization setting that preserves ImageNet accuracy preserves the model's other capabilities.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense readouts consume near-tie similarity comparisons across neighboring patches, exactly the signal structure most fragile to quantization noise.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Eight-bit vs four-bit dense-vs-global comparison on one model in a day.
core_claim: Fine-grained spatial alignment depends on small activation differences that quantization noise destroys earlier than class-level margins, so dense metrics fall off one to two bits before global metrics across models and schemes.
method_sketch: Quantize two VLMs at four bitwidths under two schemes, evaluate classification, retrieval, and dense zero-shot metrics, compare degradation onsets.
novelty_hook: Quantization robustness is well studied for classification; task-granularity-stratified analysis for dense VLM outputs appears sparse; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Results may be scheme-specific, requiring more schemes than budgeted to generalize.

title: Expression difficulty predicts safe early-exit depth for dense decoding
one_line_idea: Test whether easy referring expressions can be resolved by early-layer readouts with unchanged accuracy, enabling an expression-conditioned early-exit policy with a favorable latency-accuracy Pareto front.
problem: Dense VLM inference cost is uniform per query although query difficulty varies enormously, and no one has established whether difficulty is predictable before running the full stack.
core_hypothesis: A cheap difficulty estimator computed from the expression and early visual features predicts the minimal exit depth that preserves accuracy, and routing on it cuts average compute substantially at negligible accuracy cost.
falsifiable_prediction: The estimator-ordered exit policy achieves a strictly better latency-accuracy Pareto front than uniform-depth baselines, with large average savings; no Pareto improvement falsifies exploitable difficulty structure.
why_important: Query-adaptive compute is the main untapped efficiency axis for interactive dense systems.
why_possibly_novel: Early exits exist for classification; expression-conditioned dense early exiting appears unexplored; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument one referring model with per-layer exits, train the difficulty estimator on validation traces, evaluate the routing policy against fixed-depth baselines on two benchmarks.
main_risk: Early-layer mask quality may be uniformly poor, leaving no exploitable easy stratum.
community_default_belief: Dense decoding needs the full network for every query; adaptive depth belongs to classification.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Many expressions are single-salient-object references whose resolution plausibly stabilizes early, wasting most of the stack on them.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Per-layer readout accuracy versus a saliency-based difficulty split on one model in a day.
core_claim: A cheap difficulty estimator computed from the expression and early visual features predicts the minimal exit depth that preserves accuracy, and routing on it cuts average compute substantially at negligible accuracy cost.
method_sketch: Instrument one referring model with per-layer exits, train the difficulty estimator on validation traces, evaluate the routing policy against fixed-depth baselines on two benchmarks.
novelty_hook: Early exits exist for classification; expression-conditioned dense early exiting appears unexplored; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Early-layer mask quality may be uniformly poor, leaving no exploitable easy stratum.

title: Synonym-set embedding coverage predicts test-time prompt-expansion gains
one_line_idea: Test whether the benefit of expanding a dense query into automatically generated synonym sets at inference is predictable from the embedding-space coverage of the set, enabling principled expansion policies.
problem: Test-time prompt expansion helps rare-class dense recall inconsistently, and practitioners have no rule for when and how much to expand.
core_hypothesis: Expansion gain per class is a function of how much the synonym set enlarges the covered region of text space toward the class's visual-feature cluster, so a coverage statistic computed offline predicts per-class gains and optimal set size.
falsifiable_prediction: The coverage statistic correlates strongly with realized per-class recall gains across datasets and models, and coverage-optimized sets beat fixed-size expansion; weak correlation falsifies the predictive rule.
why_important: It converts a folklore trick into a controllable mechanism with per-query cost-benefit estimates.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt ensembling is common; a predictive coverage theory of when it works for dense recall appears new; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate synonym sets of varying sizes for benchmark vocabularies, measure per-class dense recall gains for two models, regress gains on the coverage statistic and validate the optimized policy.
main_risk: Auto-generated synonyms include near-misses whose errors may swamp the coverage signal.
community_default_belief: Prompt expansion is a small uniform win; just ensemble a handful of templates and synonyms.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Gains are demonstrably class-heterogeneous, implying an underlying structure that a uniform policy leaves on the table.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Coverage-vs-gain scatter over fifty classes on one model in a day.
core_claim: Expansion gain per class is a function of how much the synonym set enlarges the covered region of text space toward the class's visual-feature cluster, so a coverage statistic computed offline predicts per-class gains and optimal set size.
method_sketch: Generate synonym sets of varying sizes for benchmark vocabularies, measure per-class dense recall gains for two models, regress gains on the coverage statistic and validate the optimized policy.
novelty_hook: Prompt ensembling is common; a predictive coverage theory of when it works for dense recall appears new; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Auto-generated synonyms include near-misses whose errors may swamp the coverage signal.

title: Disagreement-triggered VLM invocation for streaming video referring
one_line_idea: Test whether streaming referring segmentation can run a heavy VLM only when a lightweight tracker's mask disagrees with a cheap text-visual consistency signal, cutting VLM invocations drastically at negligible accuracy cost.
problem: Video referring pipelines re-run expensive language grounding per frame or at fixed intervals, ignoring that reference assignments are stable except at discrete events.
core_hypothesis: A cheap per-frame consistency score between the propagated mask and the expression detects exactly the frames where re-grounding is needed (occlusions, referent changes, appearance shifts), so event-triggered invocation preserves accuracy with a small fraction of VLM calls.
falsifiable_prediction: Event-triggered invocation retains nearly all of per-frame-invocation accuracy (predicting above ninety-five percent) using under a fifth of the calls, beating fixed-interval baselines at matched budgets; frequent silent failures falsify the trigger signal.
why_important: It makes language-guided video segmentation feasible on edge hardware where per-frame VLM calls are impossible.
why_possibly_novel: Tracking-plus-detection scheduling is classic; a text-visual disagreement trigger for VLM invocation appears new; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build the pipeline from a public tracker and referring model, sweep trigger thresholds on video referring benchmarks, compare accuracy-vs-calls Pareto against fixed-interval scheduling.
main_risk: The consistency signal may miss gradual drift, accumulating unrecoverable tracking error between triggers.
community_default_belief: Reliable video referring requires dense temporal application of the grounding model.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Referent identity is temporally sparse information; per-frame re-grounding recomputes an answer that rarely changes.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Fixed-interval vs disagreement-triggered at matched call budgets on one benchmark in two days.
core_claim: A cheap per-frame consistency score between the propagated mask and the expression detects exactly the frames where re-grounding is needed (occlusions, referent changes, appearance shifts), so event-triggered invocation preserves accuracy with a small fraction of VLM calls.
method_sketch: Build the pipeline from a public tracker and referring model, sweep trigger thresholds on video referring benchmarks, compare accuracy-vs-calls Pareto against fixed-interval scheduling.
novelty_hook: Tracking-plus-detection scheduling is classic; a text-visual disagreement trigger for VLM invocation appears new; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: The consistency signal may miss gradual drift, accumulating unrecoverable tracking error between triggers.

title: Spatially-rich captions do disproportionate work in dense pretraining
one_line_idea: Test whether a small spatially-rich fraction of web captions accounts for a disproportionate share of dense alignment capability, making targeted curation far cheaper than uniform scaling.
problem: Web alt-text is spatially impoverished, and it is unknown whether dense capability comes from the rare spatial captions or from sheer volume of ordinary ones.
core_hypothesis: Removing the top spatially-rich decile of captions harms dense zero-shot far more than removing a random decile, while adding synthetic spatially-rich captions to a small corpus recovers much of large-corpus dense performance.
falsifiable_prediction: The spatial-decile ablation gap exceeds the random-decile gap several-fold on dense metrics while retrieval is unaffected; equal gaps falsify the disproportionate-work claim.
why_important: It would redefine data curation priorities for dense-capable pretraining, replacing volume with targeted composition.
why_possibly_novel: Data pruning research optimizes for global objectives; spatial-richness-targeted composition analysis for dense capability appears new; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Score captions for spatial richness, pretrain matched small models on ablated corpora (spatial-decile-removed, random-decile-removed, spatial-enriched), evaluate dense and global metrics.
main_risk: Small-scale pretraining may not reflect how spatial captions interact with scale.
community_default_belief: Dense capability emerges from overall data scale; caption composition is secondary.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Localization supervision can only come from text whose truth depends on position, which is a thin, identifiable slice of web data.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Fine-tune (not pretrain) one model on spatial-enriched vs random captions at matched size and compare dense deltas in three days.
core_claim: Removing the top spatially-rich decile of captions harms dense zero-shot far more than removing a random decile, while adding synthetic spatially-rich captions to a small corpus recovers much of large-corpus dense performance.
method_sketch: Score captions for spatial richness, pretrain matched small models on ablated corpora (spatial-decile-removed, random-decile-removed, spatial-enriched), evaluate dense and global metrics.
novelty_hook: Data pruning research optimizes for global objectives; spatial-richness-targeted composition analysis for dense capability appears new; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Small-scale pretraining may not reflect how spatial captions interact with scale.

title: Center-bias inheritance makes dense VLMs fail on off-center referents
one_line_idea: Quantify how photographic center bias in web training data translates into position-dependent dense grounding accuracy, and test cheap corrections (positional augmentation and readout debiasing).
problem: Web photos center their subjects, and dense VLMs may inherit a position prior that benchmark images (also center-biased) never expose.
core_hypothesis: Grounding accuracy declines measurably with referent distance from image center at matched object size and category, the decline is steeper for text-conditioned than class-conditioned models, and position-uniform augmentation during light fine-tuning flattens it.
falsifiable_prediction: Center-distance accuracy curves show significant negative slopes that augmentation flattens; flat curves out of the box falsify inherited center bias.
why_important: Robotics and surveillance images are not center-composed, so an inherited prior would silently degrade exactly the deployment domains that need grounding most.
why_possibly_novel: Center bias is known in saliency research; its quantification and correction for language-conditioned dense models appears missing; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate three models on position-controlled crops of benchmark images (same referent, shifted framing), fit accuracy-vs-eccentricity curves, test augmentation and readout corrections.
main_risk: Crop-based position control changes context visibility, confounding position with information loss.
community_default_belief: Translation-equivariant backbones make grounding position-independent up to boundary effects.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Positional embeddings and center-biased training statistics both break equivariance in ways that standard evaluations, being center-biased themselves, cannot detect.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Accuracy at three eccentricity bands for one model on shifted crops in a day.
core_claim: Grounding accuracy declines measurably with referent distance from image center at matched object size and category, the decline is steeper for text-conditioned than class-conditioned models, and position-uniform augmentation during light fine-tuning flattens it.
method_sketch: Evaluate three models on position-controlled crops of benchmark images (same referent, shifted framing), fit accuracy-vs-eccentricity curves, test augmentation and readout corrections.
novelty_hook: Center bias is known in saliency research; its quantification and correction for language-conditioned dense models appears missing; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Crop-based position control changes context visibility, confounding position with information loss.

title: Disentangling rare-mask scarcity from rare-text scarcity
one_line_idea: Determine whether rare-category dense performance is bottlenecked by scarce mask supervision or scarce textual exposure, via controlled resampling that decouples the two axes.
problem: Long-tail failures of open-vocab segmenters are blamed interchangeably on missing masks and missing text, but the axes are confounded in every existing training corpus.
core_hypothesis: For most rare categories, textual exposure is the binding constraint: adding text-only occurrences (captions mentioning the class) improves dense performance nearly as much as adding equivalent mask annotations at a fraction of the cost.
falsifiable_prediction: In a factorial resampling study, the text-axis main effect on rare-class dense accuracy approaches the mask-axis effect (predicting at least half); a dominant mask-axis effect falsifies text-bottleneck claims.
why_important: Annotation budgets for the long tail differ by orders of magnitude between captions and masks; knowing the binding axis changes data strategy economy-wide.
why_possibly_novel: Long-tail studies vary total data; the text-vs-mask factorial decoupling for dense tasks appears new; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct training corpora crossing text-occurrence count and mask count per rare class, train matched models, evaluate rare-class dense metrics, fit the factorial effects.
main_risk: Synthetic manipulation of text occurrences may inject distributional artifacts that inflate the text axis.
community_default_belief: Rare-class dense failure means we need more rare-class masks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If mask skills are class-generic and transfer, the class-specific missing ingredient is textual anchoring, which captions provide cheaply.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Two-by-two resampling for five rare classes with light fine-tuning in three days.
core_claim: For most rare categories, textual exposure is the binding constraint: adding text-only occurrences (captions mentioning the class) improves dense performance nearly as much as adding equivalent mask annotations at a fraction of the cost.
method_sketch: Construct training corpora crossing text-occurrence count and mask count per rare class, train matched models, evaluate rare-class dense metrics, fit the factorial effects.
novelty_hook: Long-tail studies vary total data; the text-vs-mask factorial decoupling for dense tasks appears new; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Synthetic manipulation of text occurrences may inject distributional artifacts that inflate the text axis.

title: Caption noise damages attribute grounding first and noun grounding last
one_line_idea: Map how increasing caption noise during training degrades different linguistic components of dense grounding, testing an ordered-fragility law (attributes before relations before nouns).
problem: Caption noise is treated as a scalar quality knob, but its damage may be linguistically structured, changing what noise-tolerant scaling actually buys.
core_hypothesis: Attribute-grounding accuracy degrades at lower noise levels than noun grounding because attribute words have weaker, less redundant visual co-occurrence signals, producing a stable fragility ordering across noise types.
falsifiable_prediction: Noise-injection sweeps show attribute grounding falling significantly earlier than noun grounding under multiple noise models; simultaneous degradation falsifies the ordered-fragility law.
why_important: If noise damage is structured, data filtering should optimize for attribute-signal preservation rather than aggregate caption quality scores.
why_possibly_novel: Noise robustness of contrastive training is studied in aggregate; a linguistically decomposed fragility analysis for dense grounding appears new; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain or fine-tune matched models under graded caption corruption (swap, drop, shuffle noise), evaluate noun, attribute, and relation dense probes per noise level.
main_risk: Different noise models may produce different orderings, complicating a single law.
community_default_belief: Caption noise uniformly dilutes supervision; a single quality threshold suffices for filtering.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Signal redundancy differs hugely across word classes, and learning theory predicts the least redundant signals drown first.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One noise type, three levels, attribute-vs-noun probes on fine-tuned models in three days.
core_claim: Attribute-grounding accuracy degrades at lower noise levels than noun grounding because attribute words have weaker, less redundant visual co-occurrence signals, producing a stable fragility ordering across noise types.
method_sketch: Pretrain or fine-tune matched models under graded caption corruption (swap, drop, shuffle noise), evaluate noun, attribute, and relation dense probes per noise level.
novelty_hook: Noise robustness of contrastive training is studied in aggregate; a linguistically decomposed fragility analysis for dense grounding appears new; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Different noise models may produce different orderings, complicating a single law.

title: Geographic grounding gaps for everyday objects in dense VLMs
one_line_idea: Measure whether dense grounding accuracy for everyday categories varies systematically with the geographic origin of the image, quantifying a deployment-equity failure that image-level audits underestimate.
problem: Geographic bias is documented for image classification, but dense grounding involves object appearance, context, and naming conventions jointly, and no pixel-level geographic audit exists.
core_hypothesis: Dense grounding of common categories (stove, bed, store) degrades significantly on images from under-represented regions, the gap exceeds the corresponding classification gap, and it concentrates in categories whose visual form varies most across regions.
falsifiable_prediction: Region-stratified dense evaluation shows gaps larger than classification gaps on matched categories, with category-level variance predicting the gap; equal or smaller gaps falsify the amplification claim.
why_important: Dense models are entering global consumer and civic applications where pixel-level failure is user-visible and consequential.
why_possibly_novel: Geographic audits exist at image level; a dense-grounding audit with amplification comparison appears new; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use geographically annotated image sources with mask annotation on sampled items, evaluate three models region-stratified on matched categories, compare against classification gaps.
main_risk: Ground-truth mask annotation across regions is the main cost and potential quality confound.
community_default_belief: Geographic bias affects which objects are recognized, and dense localization inherits it proportionally at worst.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Grounding compounds recognition with context priors and naming mismatches, three bias sources that multiply rather than average at pixel level.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Two regions, five categories, one model with lightweight annotation of two hundred items in three days.
core_claim: Dense grounding of common categories (stove, bed, store) degrades significantly on images from under-represented regions, the gap exceeds the corresponding classification gap, and it concentrates in categories whose visual form varies most across regions.
method_sketch: Use geographically annotated image sources with mask annotation on sampled items, evaluate three models region-stratified on matched categories, compare against classification gaps.
novelty_hook: Geographic audits exist at image level; a dense-grounding audit with amplification comparison appears new; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Ground-truth mask annotation across regions is the main cost and potential quality confound.

title: Sim-to-real asymmetry: synthetic data transfers relations but not attributes
one_line_idea: Test whether renderer-generated training data for dense grounding transfers to real images asymmetrically, with spatial-relation grounding transferring well while attribute grounding transfers poorly.
problem: Synthetic data is the obvious fix for rare compositional supervision, but which linguistic components survive the sim-to-real gap is unknown, so pipelines may synthesize the wrong things.
core_hypothesis: Relation grounding depends on geometry that renderers reproduce faithfully, while attribute grounding depends on appearance statistics that renderers systematically miss, producing a predictable transfer asymmetry.
falsifiable_prediction: Models fine-tuned on synthetic relation data improve real relation grounding substantially, while synthetic attribute data yields little or negative real transfer at matched scale; symmetric transfer falsifies the asymmetry.
why_important: It tells the community what synthetic dense-language data is actually worth generating at scale.
why_possibly_novel: Sim-to-real is studied per task; a linguistic-component-resolved transfer analysis for dense grounding appears new; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate matched synthetic corpora targeting relations and attributes with a modern renderer, fine-tune the same base model on each, evaluate real-image relation and attribute dense probes.
main_risk: Renderer choice strongly conditions the result; two renderers are needed to claim generality.
community_default_belief: Better renderers shrink the sim-to-real gap uniformly across supervision types.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The gap is not a scalar: geometry is nearly gap-free while material appearance remains far from photoreal, so supervision built on each inherits different gaps.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Fine-tune on existing synthetic relation datasets vs synthetic attribute recolorings and compare real transfer in three days.
core_claim: Relation grounding depends on geometry that renderers reproduce faithfully, while attribute grounding depends on appearance statistics that renderers systematically miss, producing a predictable transfer asymmetry.
method_sketch: Generate matched synthetic corpora targeting relations and attributes with a modern renderer, fine-tune the same base model on each, evaluate real-image relation and attribute dense probes.
novelty_hook: Sim-to-real is studied per task; a linguistic-component-resolved transfer analysis for dense grounding appears new; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Renderer choice strongly conditions the result; two renderers are needed to claim generality.

title: Where text-prompted unification breaks: continuous-valued dense tasks
one_line_idea: Probe whether unified text-promptable dense models fail systematically on continuous-valued tasks (depth, normals) relative to categorical tasks, because token-based text conditioning cannot express continuous targets.
problem: Unified models advertise any-dense-task-via-language, but the interface may be structurally biased toward categorical outputs, and nobody has mapped where unification actually breaks.
core_hypothesis: At matched capacity and data, text-prompted unified models show a systematically larger gap to specialists on continuous tasks than on categorical tasks, and the gap correlates with how the text interface discretizes the task specification.
falsifiable_prediction: The unified-to-specialist gap on depth and normals is several times the gap on segmentation across two unified families; equal gaps falsify the interface-bias claim.
why_important: It would define the real scope of language-driven unification and motivate hybrid interfaces before the paradigm locks in.
why_possibly_novel: Unified models report per-task numbers; a structured gap analysis attributed to interface type appears missing; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate two unified text-promptable models against matched specialists on categorical and continuous dense tasks, normalize gaps, correlate with interface discretization measures.
main_risk: Specialist baselines differ in maturity across tasks, contaminating gap normalization.
community_default_belief: Language is a universal task interface; remaining gaps reflect data and scale, not the interface.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Categorical prompts name equivalence classes, which is what language does well; continuous field prediction has no natural linguistic handle, so the interface itself is the bottleneck.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Normalized gap comparison for one unified model on segmentation vs depth in two days.
core_claim: At matched capacity and data, text-prompted unified models show a systematically larger gap to specialists on continuous tasks than on categorical tasks, and the gap correlates with how the text interface discretizes the task specification.
method_sketch: Evaluate two unified text-promptable models against matched specialists on categorical and continuous dense tasks, normalize gaps, correlate with interface discretization measures.
novelty_hook: Unified models report per-task numbers; a structured gap analysis attributed to interface type appears missing; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Specialist baselines differ in maturity across tasks, contaminating gap normalization.

title: Cycle inconsistency between segment-then-describe and describe-then-segment
one_line_idea: Measure the disagreement between running region-to-text and text-to-region directions of the same multimodal system in a cycle, and test cycle consistency as a label-free training signal for dense alignment.
problem: Dense captioning and referring segmentation are inverse tasks usually trained and evaluated separately, and their mutual consistency within one model is unmeasured and unexploited.
core_hypothesis: Current systems show large cycle inconsistency (a region described, then re-grounded, lands elsewhere), the inconsistency localizes model weaknesses without any labels, and fine-tuning on a cycle-consistency objective improves both directions on standard benchmarks.
falsifiable_prediction: Cycle IoU is far below same-direction test-retest consistency, cycle failures predict benchmark errors, and cycle training yields measurable gains in both directions; high baseline cycle consistency falsifies the exploitable-signal claim.
why_important: A label-free consistency signal would let dense models improve from unlabeled images and provide a benchmark-free diagnostic.
why_possibly_novel: Cycle consistency is classic in translation and vision; its use across the describe-ground direction pair of modern MLLMs appears underexplored; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement the cycle for two MLLM systems, quantify cycle IoU distributions on unlabeled images, correlate with benchmark errors, then fine-tune with a cycle loss and re-evaluate.
main_risk: Cycle training can converge to degenerate mutual agreement (consistent but wrong) without careful regularization.
community_default_belief: Training each direction on its own supervised data is the effective way to improve both.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Bidirectional agreement is an unsupervised correctness constraint that supervised training never enforces, leaving free signal on the table.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Cycle IoU for one model on five hundred unlabeled images in a day; near-perfect consistency ends the exploitability story.
core_claim: Current systems show large cycle inconsistency (a region described, then re-grounded, lands elsewhere), the inconsistency localizes model weaknesses without any labels, and fine-tuning on a cycle-consistency objective improves both directions on standard benchmarks.
method_sketch: Implement the cycle for two MLLM systems, quantify cycle IoU distributions on unlabeled images, correlate with benchmark errors, then fine-tune with a cycle loss and re-evaluate.
novelty_hook: Cycle consistency is classic in translation and vision; its use across the describe-ground direction pair of modern MLLMs appears underexplored; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Cycle training can converge to degenerate mutual agreement (consistent but wrong) without careful regularization.

title: Joint calibration of grounding-then-masking cascades
one_line_idea: Characterize how errors compound in box-to-mask cascades (grounding detector feeding a promptable segmenter) and test whether jointly calibrated confidence beats stage-wise thresholds at fixed compute.
problem: Grounded-SAM-style cascades dominate practical open-vocab segmentation, but stage confidences are thresholded independently, ignoring how box errors deform downstream mask quality.
core_hypothesis: Cascade failure probability is a predictable function of stage-one confidence and box-mask geometric compatibility, so a jointly calibrated accept-refine-reject policy dominates independent thresholding on the accuracy-coverage curve.
